questions.stem: What is the essential cause of thermal decomposition?

options.text: The action of heat on the substance
options.explanation: Thermal decomposition is driven by heat alone; no second reactant takes part in the breakdown.

options.text: Reaction with oxygen in the air
options.explanation: Oxygen is not needed; the carbonate already contains the oxygen that ends up in the oxide and the carbon dioxide.

options.text: Reaction with water dripping onto the solid
options.explanation: Water plays no part; the word thermal in the name points straight to heat as the cause.
options.misconception: reactant invented for a one-reactant change

options.text: The action of an electric current
options.explanation: Electrolysis is a different process; decomposition described as thermal is driven by heating alone.

questions.stem: Which pair of products results from heating a metal carbonate that decomposes?

options.text: The metal oxide and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: The carbonate gives up its carbon dioxide and leaves the metal's oxide behind, which is the pattern of record.

options.text: The metal and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: The metal itself is not freed by heating the carbonate; the solid left behind is the oxide.

options.text: The metal oxide and oxygen gas
options.explanation: The carbon leaves as carbon dioxide, not as free oxygen; the carbonate's atoms split between two products.

options.text: The metal hydroxide and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: No water is involved, so no hydroxide can form; the oxide is the solid product of the heated carbonate.

questions.stem: Which metals have carbonates that tend to decompose on heating?

options.text: Metals from the lower half of the reactivity series
options.explanation: The less reactive a metal, the less strongly its carbonate holds together, so lower-half carbonates decompose on heating.

options.text: Metals from the top of the reactivity series
options.explanation: Potassium and sodium carbonates hold together stubbornly; the very reactive metals resist this breakdown.

options.text: Only transition metals can have decomposing carbonates
options.explanation: The dividing line is the lower half of the reactivity series, not a label such as transition metal.

options.text: All metal carbonates decompose at room temperature
options.explanation: Heating is required, and the most reactive metals' carbonates resist even that; room temperature decomposes none of them.

questions.stem: Why does the breakdown of a carbonate make the solid appear to lose mass?

options.text: Because carbon dioxide escapes as a gas and is no longer part of the solid remaining
options.explanation: The gaseous product drifts away, so any solid weighed afterwards misses the mass the carbon dioxide carried off.

options.text: Because heat destroys some of the atoms
options.explanation: Atoms are conserved in every chemical reaction; the mass is not destroyed, it simply leaves as gas.

options.text: Because the metal oxide is always lighter than air
options.explanation: The oxide is an ordinary solid; the loss comes from the escaped gas, not from the oxide's weight.

options.text: Because the balance reads lower when samples are hot
options.explanation: Instrument effects are not the point; the mass genuinely leaves the sample as carbon dioxide gas.

questions.stem: A student heats sodium carbonate, from the top of the reactivity series, in a hot flame. What is the expected outcome?

options.text: Little or no breakdown, because sodium sits in the top half of the reactivity series
options.explanation: Carbonates of the most reactive metals hold together on heating, which is why the specification's example comes from the lower half.

options.text: Ready breakdown to sodium oxide and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: That behaviour belongs to lower-half carbonates; sodium's carbonate is too stable to split this easily.

options.text: The sodium metal separates out of the carbonate
options.explanation: Even decomposing carbonates leave the oxide; freeing the metal needs a different, more powerful process.

options.text: The carbonate melts but does not chemically change
options.explanation: Melting would be a physical change; the expected outcome here is that no breakdown occurs on heating.

questions.stem: What colour change is seen when copper(II) carbonate decomposes on heating?

options.text: Green solid slowly darkening to black
options.explanation: The green copper(II) carbonate becomes black copper(II) oxide as the breakdown proceeds.

options.text: Black solid turning green
options.explanation: That reverses the true order; green is the starting carbonate and black is the oxide left behind.

options.text: White solid turning blue
options.explanation: Those colours belong to other copper chemistry, such as anhydrous and hydrated copper sulfate.
options.misconception: copper colours borrowed from another topic

options.text: No colour change at all
options.explanation: The darkening is one of the clearest visible signs of this breakdown and is often the quoted observation.

questions.stem: How is the gas from the decomposing carbonate identified?

options.text: By passing it through limewater, which turns milky
options.explanation: The milky turn of limewater is the standard test that names the gas as carbon dioxide.

options.text: With a glowing splint, which relights
options.explanation: A relighting splint identifies oxygen; carbon dioxide does the opposite and extinguishes flames.

options.text: With a lit splint, which burns with a squeaky pop
options.explanation: The pop test identifies hydrogen; the carbonate's gas is carbon dioxide.

options.text: By its sharp smell in the air
options.explanation: Smelling gases is never the school test; limewater gives the safe, standard confirmation.

questions.stem: Which symbol equation describes the breakdown of copper(II) carbonate on heating?

options.text: CuCO3 (s) → CuO (s) + CO2 (g)
options.explanation: One copper, one carbon and three oxygens appear on each side, so the equation is balanced as written.

options.text: CuCO3 (s) → Cu (s) + CO2 (g)
options.explanation: The oxygen count fails: the left side has three oxygens and the right has only two; the oxide, not the metal, forms.

options.text: CuCO3 (s) → CuO (s) + CO (g)
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide has one oxygen, leaving an oxygen unaccounted for; the dioxide is the correct gas.

options.text: 2CuCO3 (s) → 2CuO (s) + 2CO (g) + O2 (g)
options.explanation: This fragments the products unnecessarily; the breakdown simply yields the oxide and carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Why does the limewater turn milky during this experiment?

options.text: Because carbon dioxide from the breakdown reacts with the limewater
options.explanation: The escaped carbon dioxide is what the limewater responds to, producing the cloudy appearance.

options.text: Because copper(II) oxide dust blows into the limewater
options.explanation: The black solid stays in the boiling tube; the milky turn belongs to the gas passing through.

options.text: Because the limewater boils in the heat
options.explanation: The limewater sits away from the flame; the cloudiness is a chemical response to the gas.
options.misconception: physical effect mistaken for the test

options.text: Because oxygen from the air dissolves in it
options.explanation: Dissolved air does not turn limewater milky; only carbon dioxide produces that signature.

questions.stem: The exam hint links cement production to rising atmospheric carbon dioxide. Which reaction in cement making mirrors this note's breakdown?

options.text: The breakdown of calcium carbonate, which releases carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Calcium carbonate behaves like copper(II) carbonate on heating, and the gas it releases adds to atmospheric carbon dioxide.

options.text: The burning of limestone in nitrogen
options.explanation: Nitrogen is not the partner; the release comes from the carbonate splitting on heating in air.

options.text: The dissolving of calcium oxide in water
options.explanation: That step follows the breakdown and releases no carbon dioxide of its own.
options.misconception: later step blamed for the gas

options.text: The rusting of iron reinforcements in concrete
options.explanation: Rusting consumes oxygen and involves no carbonate; it is unrelated to the cement-kiln chemistry.
